Our work establishes the link between these loops and induction by proving that if a particular function, $f(x)$, has an invariant that encompasses all elements of a specific interval, $[a, b]$, which involves only first-order logic, then the difference between two successive iterations of 'f(x)' over the interval will be zero. Conversely, we demonstrate that if the difference between two successive iterations of 'f(x)' is zero, then the function, $f(x)$, has an invariant that encompasses all elements of the interval, $[a, b]$. Furthermore, we provide detailed explanations and numerous examples of clause set loops, as well as a detailed example of induction that incorporates multiple loop variables.

We've developed a new class of models, called Corresponding Models, which enable knowledge transfer between linked entities. Focusing on a type of corresponding model tailored to graph retrieval tasks, we present a straightforward method to train such a model using linked graphs. We then propose two additional approaches leveraging additional knowledge about the graph structure, which can be used to further enhance the basic approach. Experimental results show that both the simple and advanced methods lead to significant and measurable improvements in graph retrieval performance, with the advanced approaches achieving better results by utilizing additional knowledge about the graph structure.

Deep learning models often struggle to effectively capture transient behavior (short-term impact) in time-series forecasting tasks. We propose that conventional training methods used in neural network-based forecasting models are largely inspired by techniques originally developed for natural language processing (NLP) models. Building on this connection, we draw upon related research in NLP to suggest new training approaches that can improve the modeling of transient effects. Our experiments with real-world data sets confirm that these novel methods significantly outperform baseline models in terms of predictive accuracy.

A critical issue in electricity distribution is ensuring that large energy users don't overburden electricity grids due to high demand. To prevent this, tiered electricity pricing is commonly used. However, research reveals that such a system can create unfair consequences for large users who are often disadvantaged due to their location and socioeconomic status. To address this issue, we introduce a novel concept of'static utility fairness,' which aims to provide a more equitable distribution of utilities among customers, while still considering the technical constraints of the grid. We develop two robust and computationally efficient algorithms that achieve'static utility fairness,' which can be integrated into existing grid infrastructure with minimal modifications.

We introduce a novel approach for resolving event coreference, focusing on events related to political controversies, and propose a one-pass dependency-based method to address this challenge. The proposed solution leverages a lightweight BERT model, trained on a minimal dataset, to enhance performance. The outcome of our approach is compared to two baseline systems, a standard pipeline and a state-of-the-art end-to-end system, and it surpasses them in accuracy, as measured by a human evaluation that supports our findings.

The Complementarity Knapsack Problem, characterized by real-valued variables and complementarity constraints, has limited application of standard linear programming techniques due to its non-differentiable objective and constraint functions. In this study, four novel types of valid inequalities are proposed for the Complementarity Knapsack Problem, namely Chordal, Triangular, Convex and Lower Bound inequalities. These new approaches are distinguished by their incorporation of complementarity constraints and the utilization of convex relaxation. A key innovation lies in converting the Complementarity Knapsack Problem into a convex programming problem by introducing a complementarity constraint. Additionally, the Chordal and Triangular inequalities are shown to be valid even in non-convex formulations, while the Convex inequality is proven to be valid for any feasible solution of the Complementarity Knapsack Problem. A computational experiment was conducted to evaluate the efficacy of the proposed approaches, demonstrating their potential to enhance the quality of lower bounds.

This paper defines and explores the concept of generalized $(m,n)$-Jordan derivations and centralizers for rings with semiprime properties, including their applicability to semiprime algebras and prime semisimple algebras. We demonstrate that all generalized derivations of semiprime rings of a certain dimension are actually within a specific class of such derivations, which we call $3\text{-}(\text{Q}_0)-$ derivations. We also investigate the properties of a certain type of derivation in non-commutative semiprime rings and show that it can be extended to a broader class of rings under a certain condition. Additionally, we prove that all generalized derivations of a certain class of non-commutative rings are actually $(1,1)$-Jordan derivations. We establish the existence of generalized $(m,n)$-Jordan derivations for various ring configurations and provide examples to illustrate the distinct properties of these derivations, including their non-equivalence with other types of derivations, which we demonstrate through counterexamples.

We demonstrate that Weinberg's 2-parameter strong coupling approach to quantum gravity can also arise in an interaction Lagrangian with only massless fields, where the fields' helicity counts play a key role. This method shows that a Lagrangian describing massive particles as point-like sources can predict the same scattering amplitudes as those calculated in a field-theoretic scenario.

We explore properties of families of nonlinear, interval-valued mappings $\mathcal{E} = \{(f_k : [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\}$. We establish conditions under which the sum of the lengths of the image transformations $f_k$ equals the total length of their range, and whether this sum converges to the total length at infinity. In doing so, we extend the Favard length concept and the properties of convergence to the total length of transformations. Additionally, we examine the convergence of the sum of lengths of single-point transformations $f_k^{-1}$ to the total length of their pre-images.

We introduce a novel, efficient guided policy search (GPS) method that leverages tube model predictive control (TMPC) for real-time imitations. The proposed approach involves a two-layered architecture, with TMPC's resilience to disturbances and adaptability to changing system dynamics at its base. TMPC's dynamic tube is continuously updated through real-time state observations and adjusts its shape based on evolving model predictions. The upper layer of the network is trained using an efficient recursive least squares solution of TMPC's optimal control problem. This results in a resilient imitator resistant to disturbances. The proposed approach significantly outperforms existing GPS methods in terms of sample efficiency, robustness, and adaptability in a cartpole benchmark scenario.

The unusual intrinsic Hall effect, characterized by an electric Hall effect without a magnetic field, is typically caused by electric currents that are not parallel to the plane of a two-dimensional electron gas. This type of effect has been discovered in a model system of this gas, where the magnetic field is applied in a direction other than parallel to the plane. This results in an electric current component not parallel to the plane, generating an electric Hall field. This field induces an electric potential that is not uniform, giving rise to electric Hall components of the current. This type of effect, occurring in the intrinsic conduction of 2D gases, is an example of an intrinsic effect. This has been also studied in more detail using a more general semiclassical theory, where the effect of scattering on these currents is considered. This theory shows that the magnitude of this effect is directly related to the average time an electron stays in the plane. This is a general property of this effect, independent of the specific details of the electron scattering.

The focus of this work is on the development of an intuitive visual representation of call graphs, allowing for the comparative analysis of multiple programs to gain a deeper understanding of call graph structures. We introduce callGraph, a novel visualization that provides a compact display of individual call graphs as well as relationships between collections of call graphs, where the structure of the visual display is grounded in the patterns found in real-world programs. We demonstrate callGraph's effectiveness through a user study, showing significant time savings when users analyze program relationships with the associated benefits of understanding call graph structures, resulting in a 261% performance boost with no adverse effects on accuracy.

The common perception that the longer training data
sequence, the better the NLP system's performance is
frequently associated with the 1B word benchmark. However, this study presents evidence suggesting that this widely cited metric is actually flawed due to its susceptibility to significant variance resulting from minor data manipulations. The research also identifies several inherent shortcomings in the metric that hinder its effectiveness. To support its claims, the study provides various experiments and examples highlighting these issues, while also discussing potential solutions to the challenges presented by the 1B word benchmark.

High-resolution microwave measurements of oscillations near flare current sheets are crucial for understanding flare magnetic field topology and energy transport. This study, based on observations from the Nobeyama Radio Observatory, focuses on low-frequency oscillations in flare loops during the M6.5 solar flare on January 4, 2021. Analyzing the spatially-resolved microwave spectra, researchers found that oscillation periods increased with microwave frequencies, and this relationship was consistent with a flare oscillation model predicting period fluctuations based on varying current density. This finding supports the "current sheet oscillation" theory, where oscillations result from the current sheet's motion, and suggests its implications for energy transport and magnetic reconnection.

In the manufacturing industry, detecting defects in products has become a critical task due to the significant economic consequences associated with production defects. Despite the prevalence of automated visual inspection, defect detection remains challenging due to the wide range of defect types and their unpredictable appearances. This paper proposes an innovative, versatile, and efficient anomaly detection method for industrial quality inspection, particularly suitable for applications with limited computational resources and the 'anomaly by design' approach. This new method diverges from traditional approaches by focusing on identifying small anomalies, as larger defects can be detected more easily and efficiently. A novel, multi-scale, and hierarchical framework is introduced to detect defects of varying sizes by iteratively applying a threshold to the input data and aggregating the resulting binary maps. This framework is designed to capture anomalies at different scales, from smaller to larger ones. The proposed method has been tested on real-world images from the Factory 2D dataset and demonstrated its effectiveness in identifying defects of various sizes. Additionally, we present an implementation of the proposed defect detection method in OpenCV under an 'A contrario' license.

We demonstrate the existence of minimal regularity solutions for the KP-I equations under a dispersion generalization. Specifically, for any fixed positive n, minimal L^2 Sobolev regularity of 3/4 + 1/p is established for solutions within the dispersion-gradient space X^s_{g}. Furthermore, our findings reveal that these solutions belong to the original space X^s for any fixed positive n, independent of the dispersion.

Kramer's theorem, which posits the degeneracy of certain states in magnetic iron oxides based on time reversal symmetry, has been challenged by experimental evidence showing significant breaching and potential degradation of this symmetry. This research aims to reconcile these findings with the theorem's predictions through an examination of degeneracy breaches in magnetic oxides, using a combination of analytical and numerical approaches based on a classical spin model of these materials. The results reveal that any significant breaches of time reversal symmetry can ultimately lead to the degeneration of these states. Furthermore, this study explores the possibility of Kramer's degeneracy reviving over time due to non-Markovian influences in the system.

In highly-mobile scenarios, predicting future CSI responses is critical for maximizing the effectiveness of online resource allocation and minimizing delay. However, existing methods are often based on short-term and unsynchronized CSI sequences, which is insufficient for making long-term predictions. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach, Long-term Recurrent Neural Network (LReNN), to predict future CSI responses for mobile massive MIMO systems. Our LReNN approach is built on a novel LSTM architecture, which incorporates a specially designed module to capture the underlying periodic changes in CSI responses. We also utilize a regularization technique to further boost the prediction accuracy. Our results demonstrate that LReNN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 50% reduction in mean absolute prediction error.

When analyzing small and/or biased samples, it's crucial to use techniques that minimize or account for sampling biases. We present a novel approach by adapting the Rao's score method to estimate homogenous and heterogenous inequality measures, specifically the Theil index, using a beta regression mixtures model. The method incorporates a latent variable to represent different inequality levels. For homogenous measures, our method shows improved robustness in biased samples. For heterogenous measures, our method utilizes a beta regression mixtures model to account for unequal inequality levels. Simulation studies confirm the method's effectiveness in handling bias and capturing real inequality patterns. The method is demonstrated with real data from a study on income inequality levels in Spain.

We investigate the asymptotic expansion at a finite distance from a point in complex projective space of the Szegő kernel's first derivative, expressed in projective coordinates and framed by the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization process, in the context of the Kaup-Kupcev metric.

The reverse line graph, a concept introduced by Rose, is a binary relationship defined by a set of edges in a graph. This relationship is established by connecting an edge in the original graph to each of its vertices on its induced path. This paper presents the Matrix Relabeling Algorithm, known as MARINLINGA, for computing reverse line graph representations. MARINLINGA is an efficient computational method that builds a reverse line graph adjacency matrix from an edge-vertex incidence matrix. MARINLINGA is compared to Roussopoulos's algorithm, an established method for constructing reverse line graph representations. The study reveals that MARINLINGA outperforms Roussopoulos's algorithm in terms of computational complexity, requiring only O(n) time. Furthermore, MARINLINGA is shown to be more effective in determining whether a graph is a reverse line graph of another graph.

This paper validates a conjecture put forward by M. Lee and M. Lee in 2001,
which pertains to the minimal degree of the defining polynomial of defectless
prime ideals in polynomial rings with a dual numbers' twist. This conjecture was
initially proposed within the context of investigating the geometry of dual
toric varieties associated with toric algebras, specifically focusing on rigid
modules. The proof we present draws upon the principles of which lemma, as
well as a generalized version of the Zariski's Factor Theorem for Macaulay
degrees.

The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) allows developers to create applications with a single, extensive dependency on the dependent module. This approach enables rapid development of new features by allowing applications to incorporate new dependencies without recompilation, but adds complexity with a growing number of dependencies over time. This research examines the long-term effects of this approach by tracking a large number of Java dependencies and their use. We found that many popular libraries are included in nearly all large-scale open-source Java projects, causing a rise in unnecessary dependencies. This use of unnecessary dependencies can be problematic as it slows down the development process and makes it harder to maintain applications. We also discovered that these issues are caused by a growing number of dependencies which are becoming increasingly interconnected. This problem is not limited to Java, but can be seen in other JVM languages such as Scala and Groovy.

We have developed a method to generate entangled biphotons in a linear optical system, utilizing photonic Glauber states that incorporate classical and quantum links between two polarization qubits. These states can be described as connected chains within the Hilbert space, with two distinct types - symmetric and anti-symmetric - that facilitate the control of quantum photonic gates. By analyzing the performance of these gates, we demonstrate their ability to efficiently perform specific operations and highlight the significance of their entangled properties in quantum information processing.

We develop methods to solve complex multistage optimization problems involving uncertainty. These problems involve uncertain distributions across stages and the objective is to minimize the worst-case outcome when distributions are unknown. A solution to this problem is referred to as an effective situation. Our research focuses on solving this problem under two specific measures: the Kullback-Leibler and the Total Variation distances. We derive insights into the nature of effective situations and develop efficient algorithms to solve these problems, specifically for a scenario involving two stages. Our research yields two main outcomes: a closed-form solution for a specific problem variant and an exact, efficient solution for a scenario involving an infinite number of stages.

Predicting future actions based on a sequence of past actions and observations is a complex task in robotics and AI. Recent studies have made significant progress in this area, but they still struggle with issues like vanishing gradients and multi-modal probability distributions. To address these challenges, we introduce a new network that uses a Rayleigh-Bernstein-Fisher (RBF-Fisher) mapping function to map high-dimensional features to a probability space. This approach offers several benefits: it ensures the output of the network lies within a probability space, facilitates gradient propagation through the network, and accommodates multi-modal distributions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, achieving a state-of-the-art performance in two benchmark datasets.

We investigate the dynamics of a system consisting of two parts, A and B, with separate Hamiltonians, connected by a time-varying interaction Hamiltonian that changes sign over a time frame t_A and stays constant for a time frame b. Using general states as initial conditions, we show that this system reaches complete thermal equilibrium within a time of approximately twice the sum of these time frames. Furthermore, we find that this time threshold is most efficiently achieved when the interaction is strongest at the midpoint between the start and end points of the time frame t_A.

We establish a criterion for the boundedness of complex-valued pseudo-differential operators on graphs that exhibit linear complexity. This leads to a determination of the conditions under which these operators are both bounded and have a nuclear property. Additionally, a specific test is developed to verify whether the Fourier transform of symbolic components falls into the space of Beurling sums.

Mobile devices are the primary users of wireless communication networks. This research investigates the impact of 5th Generation (5G) wireless networks on mobile platform-based applications, with an emphasis on spatial interactions. By comparing interactions through 4G and 5G networks, our results reveal that the exchange of data between a smartphone and nearby devices is significantly faster in a 5G environment, especially at close proximity (up to 1 meter). Conversely, our data indicates that the proximity at which data transfer is possible is reduced in a 5G setting. Additionally, our research delves into the variations in mobile network service quality, which can lead to variations in the volume of coverage (macro- or local) and ultimately affect data transfer levels.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) exhibit a tendency to be overconfident in their predictions, a phenomenon that is more pronounced when faced with out-of-distribution (OOD) instances. In an effort to mitigate this issue, we propose an adversarial method that generates OOD instances and then employs them to train and improve the accuracy of OOD detectors. Our proposed approach, known as CODES, utilizes a chamfer distance to measure the similarity between the distribution of predicted probabilities and confidence values. By doing so, it is able to produce OOD instances that are more effective in training OOD detectors. Specifically, we use the Chamfer Distance based OOD Instance Generator (CODIG) to produce these instances. In addition, we develop the Chamfer Out-of-Distribution Instances Selection (COIS) criterion to select the most informative OOD instances from these generated OOD instances. Our experiments demonstrate that CODES outperforms the state-of-the-art in OOD detection across a range of benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, and ImageNet-1000.

Measurements of the angular patterns created by subjet pairs in high-energy collisions are presented, focusing on events with two, three, and four jets. These measurements, based on data collected by the CMS detector at the Large Hadron Collider, are specifically reported for events with large transverse momentum and either one or two jets and several hundreds of GeV of net momentum in the central rapidity region. For these events, the angular patterns created by the subjet pairs are analyzed and the results are presented in different ways, such as with various parameters and by comparing to theoretical predictions. These predictions are useful for testing event generators and the results provide insights into the parton shower and hadronization, and the presence of a new interaction sector.

The recent introduction of the Deep Neural Networks (DNN) concept has significantly enhanced the capabilities of computer vision techniques. However, the necessity for a large amount of labeled training data in these computer vision deep learning methods poses a major limitation. To counteract this, researchers have developed semi-supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and self-supervised learning, which utilize limited labeled data along with unlabeled data, thereby offering efficient solutions to this problem. This study aims to provide an in-depth review of the existing deep learning-based computer vision semi-supervised, unsupervised, and self-supervised education methods, examining their characteristics, strengths, and weaknesses. Furthermore, it discusses the key challenges associated with these techniques, including the scalability issue, and highlights potential research directions to mitigate this limitation.

Row-level anomaly detection in data is a crucial task that remains relatively understudied compared to column-level detection. This challenge stems from the difficulty of capturing the internal structure of data, which is crucial for identifying anomalous rows. To address this issue, we present RECol, a novel approach that leverages reconstruction error to detect outlying rows. Building on the concept of reconstruction error, our solution utilizes the Row Embedding Model, a probabilistic graph-based approach that models row relationships. By incorporating the Monte Carlo method, we develop an efficient estimation strategy to accurately quantify reconstruction error. Furthermore, to enhance the scalability of our model, we propose an innovative sampling strategy that significantly reduces the computational cost of Monte Carlo simulations. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of RECol in outperforming existing solutions, particularly in data with structural relationships.

We establish uniformity and quantifiable results for a family of non-linear Young equations within the context of higher-order connections. Furthermore, we derive quantifiable implications for non-linear cocycles, thereby providing a resolution to open questions posed by Young. Our primary method involves a novel averaging argument, and we demonstrate the utility of our findings through the derivation of quantitative equidistribution results for non-linear cocycles on Anosov spaces with singularities.

Neutrino interactions with a magnetic field can induce a polarization of the neutrino's spin, and in turn, the neutrino's polarizability is a crucial factor in this process. For a neutrino with an energy of 10 GeV, the degree of polarization that can be achieved is relatively small, roughly 10^-20. Neutrino experiments that involve direct detection typically operate at energies under 10 GeV. As a result, the associated polarizability is a significant parameter that can be studied in these experiments. We have calculated the one-loop level corrections to the process of a charged current interaction involving an active neutrino and a final state meson, with the inclusion of a finite energy and mass for both the neutrino and meson. We have also taken into account the finite volume of the final state meson wave function and found that this factor to be approximately 1. We have discovered that the inclusion of these factors does not, however, lead to a significant enhancement in the degree of polarization.

The connection between neurons and glial cells plays a significant role in various neurological disorders, including epilepsy, Alzheimer's disease, and stroke. In our study, we examined how the synchronized activity of neurons influenced by the activity of glial cells, which consume excess neurotransmitters, can generate rhythmic patterns. We used a model that incorporated the dynamics of neurons and glial cells, as well as the release and consumption of neurotransmitters. We found that the system could produce rhythmic patterns, such as oscillations between high and low activity, depending on the levels of glutamate and its receptor activity in the neuron. We also discovered that the system could switch between different types of rhythmic patterns, and that the switching points were influenced by the parameters of the model. We compared our results to previously proposed mechanisms for rhythmic pattern switching and found that the switching was not caused by the emergence of new stable states or by changes in the symmetry of the system. Instead, we believe that the switching was due to the loss of stability of the existing rhythmic patterns, which occurred when the system encountered an unstable boundary in its parameter space.

A theoretical study focuses on the topological characteristics of a neutral spin-1/2 particle moving through a magnetic field. This analysis combines the particle's motion with the behavior of its associated Berry's vector potential. The study reveals that a magnetic field can significantly impact the system's topological properties by altering the winding numbers associated with its wave functions and the Chern numbers governing the boundary dynamics. Furthermore, this work demonstrates that the spin-1/2 particle's topological features are distinct from those of charged particles and are influenced by the magnetic field. The research also examines the topological charges of the particles' energy levels and the topological excitations under periodic translations. The study extends topological analysis to non-Abelian topological charges, which are significant for their potential uses in developing topological quantum gates.

We've developed a comprehensive, time-dependent model to analyze the expansion of a two-dimensional, radially symmetric accretion disk. This model takes into account the disk's boundary position as a function of time, considering how material is first introduced at its edge and then spreads outward through radial accretion. This approach provides a more realistic alternative to conventional models, which assume instantaneous radial flow and disregard the time it takes for material to reach the inner disk. Our new model has a simple analytical solution, allowing us to examine how changes in the disk's surface area and inner radius correlate with the accretion rate. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that the relationship between the disk's inner radius and time is not strictly linear, revealing insights into the dynamics of accretion disks in binary systems.

We establish a connection between hyperbolic L-space links and the natural number sequences lacking a square root. This relationship is leveraged to develop an efficient algorithm for determining if a given link has a hyperbolic L-space representation. Additionally, we explore the semigroups associated with these links and demonstrate that they can be viewed as subsets within specific natural number semigroups. This provides a means of identifying whether a link is an L-space link by examining the composition of its formal semigroup with the set of natural numbers.

A Poisson map linking kinetic and hydrodynamic representations of a
non-uniform medium is established, grounded in an entropy current formula proposed
by B. Derrig. This map, dependent on a kinetic equation model, yields a unique,
deterministic hydrodynamics system that is derived from the incompressible Euler equations under specific conditions. The derived system includes a universal velocity field formula, the uniform entropy hypothesis, and a uniform equilibrium distribution function. The approach can be generalized to various kinetic equation types, including collisional and collisionless systems. The resulting hydrodynamics system is shown to be globally, uniquely and exponentially stable, with its stability being influenced by the properties of the kinetic equation. Additionally, the derived systems are shown to exhibit infinite-dimensional conservative, analytic systems with this conservation analyticity.

The medical field is facing a significant challenge in processing the vast amounts of data generated from new technologies. Our research focuses on addressing this issue by exploring the potential of artificial intelligence models to assist medical staff in processing endoscopy video, specifically by detecting and removing artifacts that hinder efficient procedures. To improve the reliability of these models, we investigate the effectiveness of ensembling them and examine the impact of different ensemble methods on the task of real-time artifact detection during endoscopy procedures. Our study compares the performance of various ensemble techniques and examines their practical implications for clinical applications, with a focus on identifying optimal solutions for real-time processing requirements. Our results suggest that ensembling models can improve performance and achieve faster processing times, and we discuss the practical implications of these findings for clinical applications, including their potential for integration into clinical workflows.

This research delves into the inherent structure of source code by examining the patterns of words that make up identifier names. These so-called grammar patterns have been studied across various programming languages to understand their characteristics. By developing a systematic method for discovering and categorizing grammar patterns in a language-independent way, we aim to identify key patterns relevant to a specific context. We propose a framework for analyzing these patterns and propose criteria to determine their semantic significance. The applicability of our approach is demonstrated through its application in the programming languages Java, Haskell, Haskell macros, Python, and SQL, and we show that our method can uncover meaningful patterns with intuitive meanings.

We introduce a novel $q$-deformed $\square$-algebra, which is generated by elements $\hat{a}, \hat{b}$ under the operations $q^2\hat{a}^2$, $\hat{b}^2$, $\hat{a}\hat{b} + \hat{bhat{a}}$ and $\hat{a}^2\hat{b} + \hat{b}^2\hat{a} + q^2\hat{a}^2\hat{b} + \hat{\hat{a}^2}\hat{b}^2$. This $q$-algebra is a refinement of the $\square$-algebra, which is a sub-algebra of the $q$-shuffle algebra for the affine $\mathfrak{sl}_2$. We further introduce a $q$-deformed $\square$-module, which is parameterized by a positive integer $n$ and is based on the $\square$-algebra, and we prove that this module is isomorphic to the $q$-deformed $\square$-module of the affine $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ Lie algebra at level $n$.

The growth rate of grains in a mixture of two or more different grains is studied using a computational approach. The evolution of the grain structure is tracked over time using a numerical solver, and the resulting data is used to calibrate a set of differential equations that describe the grain-size distribution. The resulting model provides a clear and interpretable description of the grain growth process, and can be used to calculate key parameters such as the grain growth exponent and the mean grain size. The calibrated model can then be used to simulate the grain growth over time and determine the equilibrium grain size distribution.

Estimating human pose and shape from a single image has been a long-standing challenge in computer vision. Recent advances have seen significant improvements, driven by the success of certain algorithms, but ultimately limited by the specific datasets and evaluation methods used. To address this, we introduce a comprehensive benchmark that extends beyond current pose estimation methods to incorporate pose-conditional image synthesis. To facilitate this, we develop a new dataset, COCO-Human3.6K, which offers a more comprehensive evaluation of pose and shape estimation models. To enable accurate evaluation of these models, we introduce a metric that assesses the accuracy of pose reconstruction and the realism of reconstructed 3D humans. Furthermore, we provide a framework for assessing the robustness of these models to varying input conditions, including image quality, occlusion, and viewpoint. To promote future research, we make our dataset and evaluation framework publicly available.

We've investigated the phenomenon of superconductivity in a microscopic scale, specifically at sites within a network where strong electron attraction occurs. Using an Anderson-type model, we've derived an equation that describes the critical temperature of superconductivity, taking into account the effects of electron correlation and the probability of occupied and empty states at each location. Our findings suggest that, in certain conditions, superconductivity can occur even when the local occupation of certain sites would normally be expected to be one. This phenomenon becomes more pronounced as the strength of electron attraction increases and the energy cost of site occupation increases, although it is ultimately diminished by the effects of strong correlations among electrons.

We propose a comprehensive framework for converting theoretical representations of scalar leptoquark masses and mixing patterns into a single, universally applicable format. This system incorporates the full complexity of Standard Model interactions, including their interactions with other particles. It also accounts for the influence of leptoquark loops in various gauge theories like the Standard Model and in their unique extensions. The method can be applied to multiple renormalization schemes, including those used in higher-order calculations. We have developed a set of computational tools to facilitate the implementation of this framework and have made them accessible to the public through an open-source software package called LeptoQuarkTools. This package enables users to seamlessly integrate leptoquark models into their own projects, thereby streamlining the process of leptoquark model development.

The concept of categorization is fundamental to the way we navigate the world. It's a crucial aspect of learning, and a significant area of focus in Machine Learning. Despite its importance, categorization in Machine Learning often fails to account for the underlying relationships between categories. In this work, we aim to investigate these category-based connections and how they can be leveraged to improve Machine Learning outcomes. We examine theoretical frameworks for categorization, exploring how they can be applied to a range of Machine Learning challenges. By using a category theoretical approach, we develop a flexible and modular system that allows for a comprehensive understanding of hierarchical structures and the dynamic interplay between them. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this system through a range of applications, including multi-task learning, transfer learning, and feature selection. These applications highlight the utility of the proposed framework and pave the way for further research into the role of categories in Machine Learning.

This research examines terminal sliding-mode control approaches, which are reevaluated in the context of second-order systems to provide a comprehensive review of their application. A new technique, termed optimal terminal sliding-mode regulation, is proposed to achieve fast and precise control in the vicinity of a system's sliding surface. Through a case study involving a 2-degree-of-freedom robot, it is demonstrated that the introduction of an additional sliding surface can effectively mitigate the limitations of the standard terminal sliding-mode control method, which often experiences oscillations in tracking error.

This research introduces a novel non-destructive technique to evaluate the internal makeup of lithium-ion batteries by employing ultrasonic resonance techniques. The proposed method assesses both the unfastened internal structure and arrangement of lithium cobalt oxide, nickel manganese cobalt oxide, and graphite electrode layers within lithium iron phosphate based batteries. The technique measures the speed at which sound travels across these layers and uses this data to generate detailed three-dimensional visual representations. The accuracy of this technique for determining the layer thickness is demonstrated using batteries with known cell dimensions. The layer thickness determination method is then applied to a range of lithium iron phosphate batteries with varying fastened layer thicknesses. The results show that the layer thickness estimation is effective, with an average error of approximately 30 to 40% within batteries with fastened layer thicknesses of around 1.5 millimeters or greater. The proposed method also allows for non-invasive monitoring of both the internal structure and internal resistance of lithium-ion batteries. Furthermore, this technique can be applied to other types of lithium-ion batteries.

This study presents a novel control approach for a gantry crane, leveraging discrete-time flatness-based control. The system's discrete-time model is developed, and it is demonstrated that any point in the crane's position can be achieved by combining a finite number of control inputs. The control approach is divided into two stages: an infinite-horizon optimal control problem is solved to determine the best initial control value, and a finite-time stabilization issue is addressed to make the system reach the desired target position. The effectiveness of the proposed method is verified through a simulation example.

The primary source of data in training image captioning models comes from a large collection of paired images and captions. Although this approach yields impressive performance, it often results in models that rely heavily on incorrect labels. To mitigate this issue, this paper introduces the concept of cooperative knowledge distillation, where both the teacher and student models are trained simultaneously to minimize the difference in their performances under specific constraints. We present a novel framework called C-cooperative distillation, which allows both models to benefit from each other's knowledge. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our method over existing state-of-the-art techniques and support its effectiveness in handling noisy data.

We introduce a novel concept of well-linked sets of strings, offering comparisons and connections to existing theories such as combinatorial instability and the word map. Well-linked sets share similarities with Lyndon's non-autonomous words and are related to a particular case of the Thue-Morse morphism established by Arquès-Demeyer. Well-linked sets can be generated from any well-linked word through a simple, deterministic process. Furthermore, a practical algorithm is presented to identify well-linked sets of size n and to construct the well-linked words within such sets.

We define an $\mathcal{E}$-monoid as a monoid equipped with $\mathcal{E}$-subgroups for every natural number $n$, and an $\mathcal{E}$-category as a category with $\mathcal{E}$-subgroups. Given that a monoid is an $\mathcal{E}$-monoid if it meets specific criteria derived from Ehresmann, then the category associated with this monoid is an $\mathcal{E}$-category. Furthermore, the class of $\mathcal{E}$-monoids can be identified as equivalent to the class of groupoids that are $\mathcal{E}$-monoid homomorphisms. Building upon this, the class of $\mathcal{E}$-categories can be identified as equivalent to the category of $\mathcal{E}$-monoids. Additionally, the class of strict monoids is identified as a particular instance of the class of $\mathcal{E}$-monoids.

Recent self-attention models have demonstrated remarkable performance across various tasks, yet their fundamental principles remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigate the critical depth-to-width interaction through a theoretical framework, revealing that the number of attention heads and the total token interaction count grow exponentially with depth, albeit at a slower rate controlled by the width. The findings imply that increasing depth allows representations to interact with more tokens exponentially, ultimately leading to an infinite loop if width remains constant. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a regularization technique that promotes diversity in token interaction, enabling the model to identify more relevant tokens for improved performance. The findings are substantiated through experiments on multiple datasets.

The development of multiferroic BiFeO$_{3}$ nanoparticles with a single phase has been successfully achieved through a modified hydrothermal method at a relatively low temperature of 170~$^{\circ}$C. The resulting BFO nanoparticles possessed a uniform size of $\sim$30~nm and exhibited multiferroic properties as evidenced by both X-ray and neutron diffraction analysis. The presence of a ferroelectric and magnetic phase transition was confirmed through neutron diffraction, with the ferroelectric phase transitioning at 650~K and the antiferromagnetic phase at 380~K. The BFO nanoparticles demonstrated enhanced magnetization and superior optical responsiveness, as well as excellent crystallinity and electrical conductivity. The BFO nanoparticles also exhibited significant activity in the degradation of methylene blue, with a rate constant of 6.0$\times$10$^{-3}$~mol~L$^{-1}$~s$^{-1}$. Notably, the BFO nanoparticles outperformed a commercial Pt/TiO$_{2}$ catalyst in hydrogen evolution, with a rate of 2.0~$\mu$mol~h$^{-1}$. The findings suggest that the BFO nanoparticles could be a valuable resource for the development of eco-friendly hydrogen production technology.

Within an extended ${\rm SU}(6)$ flavor framework, where the standard model is augmented by vector-like doublets, we examine the masses of bottom quarks and tau leptons. This analysis reveals that the masses at the standard model scale originate from a combination of Yukawa interactions tied to ${\rm SU}(6)$ flavor violations. Furthermore, our investigation into the evolution of these masses from the Planck scale down to the standard model reveals that the evolution constants associated with bottom quarks and tau leptons are non-universal.

In our research, we focus on accurately recreating the three-dimensional shape of various objects
when they are held in an image by a single camera. Existing methods rely on specific object categories
or require additional information such as color or depth data. Our approach uses a two-stage deep learning
network that generates an initial 3D shape estimate by predicting a set of predefined vertices, followed by a
vertex-based deformation module that refines this estimate using image features and 2D keypoint projections
associated with the initial prediction. Notably, our method can handle a wide range of objects without needing
to identify specific object categories or use any additional data.

The Ca-K index, a crucial solar parameter, has been utilized in forecasting solar weather and correlating with solar irradiance fluctuations. This study leverages a century-long dataset of daily Ca-K images from the Kodaikanal Observatory to examine the connections between the Ca-K index and solar activity indicators. The results reveal that the Ca-K index is significantly influenced by sunspot area and sunspot number, with correlation coefficients reaching 0.99 and 0.94, respectively. The study also investigates the temporal variations of the Ca-K index and sunspot number over long and short periods using wavelet analysis and power spectrum density techniques. The findings suggest that the long-term fluctuations in the Ca-K index and sunspot number exhibit similar behavior, while short-term fluctuations follow a red noise pattern, indicating that there is a strong link between the Ca-K index and solar cycle activity indicators.

The interaction between the up quark and the sigma baryon is a key parameter in understanding the strong force between particles. However, the current experimental data on its decay to a proton and a pair of muons is still missing. This study presents the first evidence of a decay from LHCb's muon spectrum data, and we also provide an estimation of the branching fraction for this specific transformation.

A new distributed approach for evaluating symbolic expressions is introduced, which divides the complex process into manageable sub-tasks by determining a standard level of detail for each step. Each receiver processes the symbolic expressions using the established criteria, combining the results into a comprehensive set of assessments. The effectiveness of this novel framework is compared to existing protocols in an exhaustive study of its performance, with the results revealing substantial improvements over non-distributed methods. Specifically, the distributed strategy can process a larger variety of symbolic expressions at comparable speeds, or evaluate the same expressions faster than non-distributed assessment.

The changes associated with the relaxation in a systematically arranged magnetic nanoparticle arrangement are examined through the lens of the Glauber model, which focuses on the single-spin transformations within the Ising model. This systematic arrangement results in a more intricate energy map for the system, which we have explored in terms of the nanoparticle spacing and temperature. Notably, our findings reveal that both temperature and interparticle distance have a substantial impact on the system's tendency to skip single-spin transformations, with close-packed nanoparticle arrangements exhibiting a significant decrease in the rate of these single-spin relaxations.

A central server-based approach is often employed in multi-device learning to aggregate local model updates, but using this method raises significant concerns about personal data protection. To address this limitation, a new, central server-free federated learning framework is proposed in this paper, enabling decentralized model training in scenarios where no central authority exists. The framework relies on a novel, efficient, and secure aggregation protocol using reconfigurable linear codes, allowing for both performance improvements and security enhancements against potential adversaries. The protocol's analysis reveals its effectiveness in achieving accuracy within a certain margin of the optimal, centrally managed solution while reducing communication costs. The results demonstrate that the reconfigurable linear code-based approach outperforms existing methods, especially in low signal-to-noise ratio environments.

This paper investigates how to effectively categorize sequential texts of limited length using advanced models like RNNs and CNNs. We propose a new approach that integrates RNNs and CNNs to capture the long-term dependencies in each sequence. We present two methods to utilize RNNs in optimizing both hidden state representations for prediction and temporal ordering of texts. We also introduce a new technique to dynamically select key features from each document based on its first few words, and use these in a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to derive a final representation. We demonstrate the strengths of our proposed approach over existing methods in benchmark datasets, and show that it performs well on real-world tasks such as Twitter spam detection and sentiment analysis.

A comprehensive analytical formulation for telecentric etalons in optical systems is developed, taking into account the etalon's thinness and the potential for non-linear phase modifications. This analytical model serves as a foundation to investigate the impact of etalon thickness on various optical systems. Derivations for etalon thinness adjustments are provided, along with the corresponding impact on linear and non-linear optical system performance. Additionally, the formulation is extended to include multi-layered etalons and the associated linear and non-linear performance effects associated with them.

The existence of solutions in the consistent matching problem is guaranteed if the set of receivers has a unitary width, a property also necessary for the existence of solutions in the more general consistent set cover and consistent set packing problems. Solutions can be found efficiently through a reduction to a similar graph structure with a reduced number of elements. Consistent matchings in bipartite graphs correspond to specific paths in hypercubes, and a linear algorithm exists to construct a maximum-sized solution. The existence of solutions in the consistent matching problem is NP-hard, and the difficulty of computing the minimum and maximum sizes of subgraphs in bipartite graphs is resolved, with the minimum size problem being solvable in quadratic time and the maximum size problem being solvable in linear time.

As interest in monolithic chiplets grows, the need for standardized interfaces, tools, and software frameworks that enable seamless integration with ASICs and FPGAs has become a priority. To facilitate this integration, the Codelet Framework has been developed to provide a standardized interface for these heterogeneous accelerators, allowing users to write portable, FDU-specific code and high-level, platform-independent code. The Codelet framework is expected to play a crucial role in the adoption of chiplets by addressing the software challenges associated with their integration.

A novel approach to parameter estimation for the finite mixture model with a nonparametric component has been proposed, particularly for the mixture cure model. This estimation method involves iteratively applying smoothing procedures, starting with an initial parametric model, and then transitioning to a more general one. This approach is established for the inverse proportional hazard model, and the resulting estimators are shown to be consistent and asymptotically normal. Furthermore, the performance of the proposed method has been numerically verified through simulation experiments.

The entropy production rate $\mu$ is a key characteristic of random walks on a graph, linking the past and future vertices at any given time $t$. It's known that random walks converge to a stationary distribution, which defines the measure dimension $s$ of the graph, representing the length of the smallest paths between typical points. This paper explores the nonlocal measure dimension $s^{\mathrm{nl}}$, which expands the conventional measure dimension $s$. We find that $s^{\mathrm{nl}}$ equals the smallest dimension $s_0$ and $s_1$ representing the length of the shortest and second shortest paths between vertices in the graph, with $s_0\le s\le s_1$. For connected, aperiodic graphs with symmetric transition probabilities, $s_0$ equals the Cheeger constant and $s_1$ equals the Cheeger constant squared. In particular, for planar graphs, $s_0$ equals 0 and $s_1$ equals 4.

In-memory computing systems focus on minimizing data transfer between processing and memory components to achieve high efficiency. This paper explores a side-channel assault on in-memory computing architectures, which exploits predictable patterns in memory access. The proposed assault, utilizing a timing analysis technique, targets memory controllers that optimize data retrieval. The results show that with basic equipment and minimal data, it's possible to achieve an assault success rate of almost 100% and accurately predict 92% of the data bits within 10 attempts.

We have developed a new method for calculating the reduced electron polarization for single nucleon emission in $^{18}$F beta decay. This method enables the extraction of the reduced kernel from experimental data, which can then be compared to theoretical models of the decay process. Our analysis includes a thorough examination of the dependence of the reduced kernel on the electron energy and the angle of the electron emission. We have derived a set of mathematical equations to model this kernel, involving a series of angular coefficients and coefficients that describe the interaction between the initial and final nuclear states. These equations can be applied to any nuclear state and are independent of the specific decay mechanism governing the process.

A novel, self-supervised approach to noise reduction in seismic data is developed, leveraging a U-net model with transfer learning. By fine-tuning the model for new datasets, transfer learning enables improved results without requiring extensive training on novel datasets. This method is further enhanced by incorporating a U-net-based data generation technique that simulates real seismic patterns from synthetic data, thereby increasing the size of available training data. This U-net model is applied to a blind-spot seismic source classifying task and successfully eliminates background noise. By utilizing transfer learning and data augmentation, the method achieves a high classification accuracy of 95.5% on a blind-spot seismic source dataset, significantly outperforming traditional noise reduction techniques. This research presents an innovative solution for self-supervised noise reduction in seismic data and demonstrates the effectiveness of transfer learning and data augmentation strategies.

The chiral quark-spectator model has been used to calculate the charge-asymmetric correlations in the final state of elastic lepton- and antilepton-nucleon scattering. This method involves considering the real photon emission process, allowing for the determination of the ratio of specific cross-section components. Findings show that the ratio of the cross-section components remains unchanged at high momentum transfers. Furthermore, the cross-section components exhibit a certain level of statistical correlation. Our research has also explored the implications of these results for the measurement of the proton and neutron tensor polarizabilities, particularly in elastic lepton- and antilepton-nucleon scattering. Notably, the observed charge-asymmetric correlations may introduce systematic errors in future tensor polarizability measurements.

We investigate the low-energy excitations in Sr$_2$Ir$_{1-x}$Sc$_x$O$_4$ using scanning tunneling spectroscopy, which allows us to study the evolution of the spectrum as Sc doping increases. In the undoped compound, our data show a consistent spin-polaron ladder spectrum, whereas at higher Sc concentrations, we observe a shift towards a spin-polaron spectrum. These results are in line with theoretical predictions and highlight how scanning tunneling spectroscopy can be a powerful tool for identifying spin-polaron and spin-ladder spectra in doped Mott semiconductors, even when the dopant is weak.

In recent years, mediation analysis has gained significant attention for its capacity to uncover the influence of a treatment on an outcome through intermediate factors. This information enables researchers to attribute the observed effects in a more transparent and accountable manner. Assuming a treatment has a continuous value, this study develops a novel framework for assessing mediation through a multiple robust approach. This involves defining a mediation effect that is uncorrelated with confounding factors. We derive an estimator for this effect by integrating a local linear least squares estimator and local quadratic least squares estimator under minimal assumptions. This estimator is consistent and converges at a central limit theorem rate, making it suitable for analysis. This framework is further extended to incorporate multiple mediators and demonstrates the efficacy of the method in a simulation study and a real-world application involving an investigation of how parental education affects children's cognitive abilities via maternal stress levels.

This Special Issue of the IEEE Transactions on Antennas and Propagation focuses on starships in the design of antennas, with an extensive history dating back to the 1950s. The issue features comprehensive technical contributions that will provide a solid foundation for exploring various starship applications. The introduction highlights notable past achievements, such as the development of large aperture antennas for satellite communication systems, as well as the insights gained from these projects. The introduction also forecasts future developments in the field, which includes the integration of starships with other antenna design methods. The introduction concludes with its assessment of the significance of this Special Issue.

A significant number of individuals struggle with suicidal thoughts, underscoring the importance of accessible and effective support systems. Consequently, there is a growing need for precise and reliable data to inform research, especially in suicidal prevention efforts. To address this challenge, we have compiled the Robin dataset – a comprehensive online collection of suicidal text. This dataset encompasses text data from online platforms such as Twitter, Reddit, and Grindr, offering a detailed and nuanced understanding of individuals expressing suicidal thoughts. Notably, our collection is distinct from existing alternatives due to its focus on explicit suicidal language, scalability, and the incorporation of various relevant online platforms. This, in turn, enables researchers to adapt and refine established methods for detecting suicidal thoughts and refining mental health classification models.

This research examines a unique classical mechanical system characterized by a novel potential function, denoted as $V_{\bf Zwart}$. The study of this system, referred to as superZwartian mechanics, focuses on its behavior under the influence of $V_{\bf Zwart}$. The investigation into the superZwartian system reveals that it exhibits characteristics similar to the quartic two-dimensional oscillator, featuring bounded trajectories and periodic motion patterns. The study also delves into the first integrals and conservation laws of the superZwartian system and discovers connections to the parametric Zwartian system, where a distinct potential function, $V_{\rm Zwart}^{\rm par}$, is involved. The findings suggest that the parametric Zwartian system can be seen as an altered superZwartian system, resulting from a specific transformation that alters its inherent properties.

The article focuses on examining the stability analysis and boundedness solutions of a novel nonlinear difference equation model. This equation has significant applications, particularly in medicine during the current Coronavirus Pandemic. We employ the Krasucki-Quinn method to assess boundedness solutions, building upon a prior work by Dhal and Kar.

We examine a set of charged black hole solutions within a 4-dimensional spacetime, derived from a specific model of non-linear electrodynamics that includes a general quadratic term within a restriction on the electromagnetic potential. These spacetime solutions are generated from a specific metric solution to a non-linear electrodynamics model in the presence of a magnetic field, X, with the charge parameter, ν, acting as a bridge between models of non-linear electrodynamics that conserve electric charge. For a particular value of the magnetic field, the general model reduces to one of two well-known models of non-linear electrodynamics. By employing the principle of the Smarr relation, we investigate the first law of black hole mechanics under variations in the magnetic field and magnetic charge.

A collection of n linear combinations of the unit vector is considered Sidon if any two of these combinations, multiplied by non-negative integers, wouldn't both equal zero unless the combinations match. We define a specific type of Sidon collection as a "zero-free Sidon collection" if it can be represented as a set of n linear combinations of the unit vector where each combination equals a positive integer. Our research demonstrates that a zero-free Sidon collection exists for any n equals 3 and k equals 2 but not for n equals 4 and k equals 2, or n equals 4 and k equals 3, or n equals 5 and k equals 3.

The scaling theory of critical phenomena has been applied to calculate magnetic susceptibility at finite temperatures for the XY spin model in its uniform polarized phase. This approach has been further extended to the nonuniform polarized phase, where the geometric phase was studied alongside susceptibility, yielding notable results regarding the scaling behavior of topological properties near critical points. Notably, the scaling dimension of the geometric phase at the critical point was found to be one, indicating a characteristic feature of its universal behavior.

We investigated the dynamics of Ising ferromagnets in a $d$-dimensional cubic lattice with three-spin exchange interaction. Using Monte Carlo simulations, we explored the dynamics of a 3D Ising model for systems with 2.2 million spins where the temperature was reduced at a near constant cooling rate. Observing that the relaxation time increased logarithmically with age in two-dimensional systems, we were surprised to discover that in three-dimensional Ising models, the relaxation time actually decreases as the system ages. This phenomenon can be attributed to the fact that a three-dimensional ferromagnet forms more quickly than a two-dimensional one, and our results suggest that a hotter ferromagnet should relax more quickly.

In one-dimensional quasicrystals characterized by a quasiperiodic potential, localized pairs of particles are stable even when subjected to power-law hopping, which occurs in certain models. The emergence of these localized pairs is due to the balance between quasiperiodic fluctuations and power-law hopping, and their stability is also influenced by the presence of a power-law distribution of single-particle localizations. Our research indicates that the probability of a localized pair scales exponentially with distance under these conditions, provided that the power of the power-law hopping is greater than one. Furthermore, pairs of particles with varying labels can also occur, and we find that the probability distribution of these pairs follows a thermal equilibrium form.

Human-computer interaction has been driven by dialogue as a crucial means of interaction for decades, with significant advancements in artificial intelligence, human-centered interaction, and language processing. The development of dialogue systems has long been hindered by the challenge of moving beyond English and across language and task boundaries, including non-English multilingual systems and tasks with varying levels of complexity. The integration of artificial intelligence and human-centered design has been hindered by the limitations of natural language processing, particularly in efficiently processing and reusing user data, creating a significant gap in the development of effective dialogue systems. This paper presents an overview of the current state-of-the-art in dialogue system development, with a focus on the challenges and opportunities presented by the use of natural language processing to bridge the gap and improve dialogue system development between languages and across different task domains.

The expression of alternative forms of genes, specifically those with multiple exons, is regulated by a complex interplay of factors influencing splicing. To better understand the dynamics of short-term changes in gene expression, we analyzed RNA sequencing data from a study on mice that were subjected to cold stress. We developed a new computational method to identify genes with multiple exons that show differential splicing, either by adding or removing exons, from this experimental data. The results revealed that cold stress caused significant changes in the splicing of over a thousand genes, which were further categorized into two types of differential splicing events. These were found to be involved in a wide range of biological processes, including the adaptation to new environments and cellular responses to stress. The genes that show differential splicing due to the addition or removal of exons at the 5' or 3' boundaries of transcripts were found to exhibit distinct patterns of regulation. The genes that show the rapid addition of exons at the 3' boundary were found to exhibit rapid changes in gene expression, whereas those showing the rapid removal of exons at the 5' boundary exhibited long-term changes in gene expression. The rapid regulation of splicing, particularly the rapid addition of exons at the 3' boundary, suggests that alternative splicing may be a key mechanism for regulating gene expression in response to environmental changes.

In response to the Facebook-Cambridge Analytic data privacy scandal, governments worldwide introduced stringent regulatory requirements governing data privacy compliance. Although numerous studies have focused on the impact of these laws on businesses, there is a lack of understanding regarding how companies integrate these requirements within their existing systems. This study aims to address this knowledge gap by examining the measures taken by companies to achieve data privacy compliance, from initial steps to long-term implementation. Through in-depth interviews with 19 IT and compliance professionals, we explored their experiences with implementing technical data privacy measures and uncovered three distinct phases in the implementation process - preparation, integration, and refinement - each characterized by distinct challenges. By gaining a deeper understanding of these challenges, we provide recommendations to businesses and offer suggestions for future research directions that align with the long-term objectives of this qualitative study.

The azimuthal angular distributions of charged hadrons in pA collisions are examined, with a focus on how the event plane of the projectile nucleus influences the distributions. A consistent pattern emerges, showing that the most forward hadrons align with the event plane, while a reverse trend is observed for hadrons with the event plane to the left or right of them. This phenomenon is also present in pp and pA collisions at similar multiplicities, and is attributed to the effects of the projectile nucleus's field. This suggests that the observed pattern is not a result of the final state, and is instead an indication that the angular distributions are influenced by the Wigner distribution of the projectile nucleus's field. A possible method for utilizing this effect to gain insight into the Wigner distribution of the projectile nucleus's field is proposed.

The formation of light nuclei in high-energy collisions is influenced by a complex interplay of processes including the interplay of nucleons, the interplay of interquarks, and the intercorpuscular interplay of quarks and gluons.  In particular, the interplay of quarks and gluons is crucial for understanding the formation of nucleons and their light variants, and is also a key factor in the formation of protons and their light variants.  In this study, we examine the formation of light particles in collisions of gold and gold at an energy of 3 GeV, using a model of microscopic collisions known as AMPT with a combination of interquark and intercorpuscular interplay.  We find that the model's predictions for light particle formation are consistent with current data, and that the model's different mechanisms for particle production have distinct effects on light particle spectra.  Furthermore, we find that the intercorpuscular interplay is the dominant mechanism for particle production at small and large distances from the collision point, while the interplay of nucleons and quarks has a more moderate influence.  We also find that the model's light particle spectra are consistent with current data on particle spectra in collisions of gold and gold at this energy.

The discovery of numerous exoplanets has given rise to a new generation of research focused on determining the characteristics of these celestial bodies. Specifically, there is a pressing need to understand the conditions surrounding rocky planets similar to Earth. This knowledge will be essential in comprehending the processes that shape the chemical composition of rocky planets and ultimately, in making informed predictions about the likelihood of finding life beyond our solar system. This review delves into the current state of the field, examining the core issues that need to be addressed. Furthermore, it surveys the most up-to-date research findings and presents the most widely accepted theories, while also identifying the unresolved mysteries and areas requiring further investigation. Ultimately, it offers a foundation for the research that will be presented in the subsequent chapters of this volume.

The property of dispersibility for a set of graphs connected through a central vertex holds if any vertex in the set can generate a unique, high-degree subgraph within the given graph. We demonstrate the dispersibility of specific circulant graphs for a given set of central vertices. These findings have applications in the field of cryptographic key distribution through thoroughly connected networks.

This study presents an enhanced iterative matrix inversion method, tailored for implementation on GPU hardware to capitalize on its acceleration potential. The original work of this paper has been expanded to accommodate arbitrary order techniques, with a focus on optimizing the speed and efficiency of iterative inversion in the context of GPU computing. Theoretical analysis confirms the convergence of these algorithms, and the efficacy of the novel methods is demonstrated through numerical simulations. The results indicate that these algorithms are well-suited for rapid matrix inversion applications, such as channel equalization, and are particularly effective when dealing with large matrices that cannot be fully loaded into the GPU's memory. The techniques proposed here offer substantial speedup potential, achieving up to 80% acceleration over conventional CPU-based methods, with a relative error of 10^-3 or 10^-4. The findings of this study provide valuable insights into the design and optimization of iterative matrix inversion algorithms, with a view to future hardware acceleration using GPU technology.

We examine the power spectrum $P(k)$ of primordial fluctuations for single-field inflation models with ultra-slow-roll, taking into account the impact of quantum back reaction. Our analysis utilizes a cosmological perturbation framework based on a multiple-time-scale expansion method, which enables us to compute the power spectrum up to the Hubble horizon scale. The study demonstrates that quantum back reaction significantly alters the power spectrum compared to the tree-level model, particularly at large values of $k$. Furthermore, the paper investigates the running of spectral index $n_s$ and finds that quantum back reaction can lead to a non-zero value of $n_s$ at large $k$.

We introduce the Enhanced Assortment Optimization problem, a highly challenging combinatorial optimization issue. Specifically, we aim to select a set of items from a given product catalog to be displayed online. This selection should meet certain criteria: (1) the total number of items should be minimized, (2) the optimal revenue generated from each item should be maximized, and (3) the total weight of selected items should be optimized. This problem is motivated by scenarios in e-commerce and logistics, where it has practical applications. We investigate the Enhanced Assortment Optimization problem from a computational perspective, examining both its theoretical and empirical aspects. Notably, we prove that the problem is NP-hard, introduce a new linear programming relaxation, and show that it is a powerful approximation algorithm. We also develop a more efficient approximation algorithm, which significantly outperforms a state-of-the-art baseline approach on a range of datasets, leading to improved solution quality.

The casebase model-based estimate is a competing risk at-risk model that calculates the probability of an event occurring up to a defined time point. It's particularly useful for survival examinations and comparing event rates across distinct groups. We introduce an innovative method to estimate this parameter using a non-parametric approach. This approach replaces the traditional maximum likelihood method, which requires re-formulating the problem. Our method offers a straightforward solution through a simple algorithm. We also provide a method to estimate the associated uncertainty. We validate the effectiveness of this method using a publicly available dataset.

This study presents a computational tool for analyzing Feynman integrals with loops and complex dimensions. The tool, known as Impact, can evaluate integrals based on either property-based integration or multi-term ansatzes. By employing impact, significant advancements have been achieved in two key areas. Firstly, the tool has been utilized to derive all relevant Feynman integrals for Higgs boson production through gluon fusion in scenarios involving four or five precise mass scales. Secondly, the tool has been applied to a two-loop analysis of Higgs boson production within gluon chains, resulting in the accurate determination of relevant Feynman integrals for scenarios involving four mass scales.

This study compares the performance of two data management systems, Lustre and DAOS, in object-based and file-based architectures. By integrating a Lustre client and DAOS client into a parallel program, we evaluate the effect of data management choices on application performance. Our findings show that Lustre and DAOS have similar bandwidth utilization. A comprehensive benchmarking of these systems reveals that Lustre's performance is hampered in certain scenarios due to its object access methods, leading to lower performance compared to DAOS. Our study also reveals that adjusting Lustre's access patterns can temporarily mitigate these performance issues.

The growing adoption of electric vehicles has resulted in the development of public electric vehicle charging stations. These stations are equipped with multiple charging points to cater to a substantial number of users. However, this situation creates security and privacy concerns, particularly in environments where unauthorised individuals may access and use the charging facilities. To address this, this study proposes an access control system that enables users to charge their vehicles efficiently while ensuring secure operation. The proposed system is designed to provide users with a priority charging service, ensuring that vehicles without fully charged batteries receive the available power. Based on a blockchain network, the system prevents users from manipulating the power distribution, thus promoting fairness. To provide enhanced security, the system further incorporates a secure protocol for authentication and authentication revocation, thus limiting any potential risks. An evaluation of the system's performance was conducted, indicating its feasibility and efficiency.

This research paper explores linear codes with unique dual properties, known as dual LCD (not fully explored until 2019) and their dual of dual (DD) properties, along with proposed applications. The study delves into distinct types of dual LCD codes and presents findings on their structure and rate of occurrence. The investigation extends to finding generalized dual LCD and DD codes, and examines their connection to specific types of linear codes. The researchers also introduce new forms of linear codes – extended, augmented, and new augmented dual LCD codes – and analyze their structure. The paper concludes by investigating self-dual LCD codes and their rate of occurrence.

The Equivalence Theorem, a cornerstone of General Relativity, asserts that GR can be viewed as the non-linear generalization of Linearized Gravity. Building on this concept, we've discovered that the theorem extends to loop corrections to quantum amplitudes, as long as they're governed by the BFKV relations. This implies that the loop corrections to linearized theory yield the same corrections to GR as the one-loop corrections to the same theory. To calculate these loop corrections, we're leveraging the techniques developed for computing corrections to the Correlation Function of the Stress-Energy Tensor in the context of AdS/CFT correspondence.
